findings.title: _getRewards Always Returns Zero During Unstake Due to Premature Balance Zeroing
findings.description: In `_unstake()`, the validator's balance is zeroed on line 186 (`info.balance = 0`) before `_getRewards()` is called on line 193. Since `_getRewards()` reads `stakeInfo[validatorAddress].balance` from storage (now 0), it always returns 0. The consequence is that `distributeStakeReward` is called with `rewardAmount=0` and `msg.value=bal` (the full stake+rewards), meaning the entire payout comes from ConsensusRegistry's TEL pool rather than splitting between ConsensusRegistry (for stake) and Issuance (for rewards). This leads to systematic insolvency of the ConsensusRegistry.

findings.title: applyIncentives Inflates Validator Balance Without Backing TEL Transfer
findings.description: `applyIncentives()` increases `stakeInfo[].balance` without any TEL transfer (line 85). The rewards are purely accounting entries. Combined with the order-of-operations bug in `_unstake()` (VULN-001), the phantom rewards created by `applyIncentives` are sourced from ConsensusRegistry's stake pool during unstake, creating systematic insolvency as rewards are debited from other validators' stakes.

findings.title: Protocol Halt from ConsensusRegistry Insolvency Causing applySlashes to Revert
findings.description: The compounding effect of VULN-001 and VULN-005 causes `applySlashes` to revert when ConsensusRegistry becomes insolvent. When `_consensusBurn` triggers `_unstake()`, it sends `{value: bal}` including phantom rewards. If ConsensusRegistry lacks sufficient TEL, the EVM reverts with insufficient balance, violating the critical invariant that system calls must never revert, and halting epoch progression across the entire Telcoin Network.

findings.title: setBufferSize Fails to Pad ringBuffer When Growing, Causing Out-of-Bounds Access
findings.description: When `setBufferSize()` is called with `newSize > bufferSize`, the function copies existing items to the new buffer but does not pad to the new size. After execution, `ringBuffer.length == oldSize` but `head == oldSize`, causing the next `attestGitCommitHash` call to access `ringBuffer[oldSize]` — an out-of-bounds index — permanently reverting until an admin calls `setBufferSize` again. This effectively bricks the attestation system.

findings.title: Silent Failure on Slashed TEL Consolidation to Issuance
findings.description: The return value of the low-level call to send slashed TEL to Issuance is discarded: `(bool r,) = issuance.call{value: stakeAmt - bal}(""); r;`. The standalone `r;` is a no-op expression. If the transfer fails, slashed TEL remains locked in ConsensusRegistry with no accounting entry and no revert, leading to permanently locked funds.

findings.title: uint8 Overflow in setBufferSize Ring Buffer Arithmetic Causes DoS
findings.description: The expression `(start + i) % bufferSize` performs addition on two `uint8` values. In Solidity 0.8+, checked arithmetic applies at the declared type. When `start + i > 255`, the operation reverts with an overflow, making `setBufferSize` uncallable for certain ring buffer states.

findings.title: Delegation Nonce Never Advances Due to Struct Overwrite
findings.description: Post-increment on line 211 is undone by a full struct overwrite on line 224. The nonce stays at 0 permanently. Currently mitigated by a one-time Undefined status check, but the nonce mechanism is broken for any future changes that rely on nonce uniqueness.

findings.title: Precision Loss in Reward Distribution Due to Two-Step Division Truncation
findings.description: Two-step division truncation in reward calculation in `applyIncentives()`. PRECISION_FACTOR (1e32) minimizes but does not eliminate dust. Undistributed dust accumulates per epoch, leading to gradual underallocation of rewards over time.

findings.title: applyIncentives Does Not Verify Validator Is Active
findings.description: `applyIncentives()` only checks `tokenId == UNSTAKED` but not `ValidatorStatus.Active`. It relies on off-chain protocol client to exclude non-active validators from rewardInfos. A malformed or malicious incentive payload could credit rewards to non-active validators.

findings.title: Permit Front-Running DoS on permitWrap()
findings.description: Classic ERC-2612 permit front-running: an attacker can extract the permit signature from the mempool and call `wTEL.permit()` first, causing the victim's `permitWrap()` to revert on the permit call. No fund loss occurs, but the transaction fails. Fix: wrap the permit call in a try/catch block.

findings.title: Burned Event Emits Pre-Truncation Amount, Causing Off-Chain Overcounting
findings.description: `Burned(from, nativeAmount)` uses the original pre-truncation value. The actual bridged amount is `nativeAmount - remainder`. Off-chain indexers and bridge relayers that rely on this event will overcount the amount burned, potentially leading to incorrect bridge accounting.

findings.title: unsettledRecords() Unbounded Iteration Can Cause Out-of-Gas
findings.description: The view function `unsettledRecords()` iterates a linked list with no bound. Acknowledged in NatSpec. For accounts with many unsettled records, this can run out of gas, making the view function unusable for those accounts.

findings.title: doubleWrap() Accepts Sub-Bridging-Threshold Amounts That Cannot Be Bridged
findings.description: There is no minimum amount check in `doubleWrap()`. Amounts below `DECIMALS_CONVERTER` (1e16) can be wrapped but never bridged, creating a UX trap. While funds are not permanently lost (unwrap path exists), users may believe their tokens are bridgeable when they are not.

findings.title: permitWrap() is Payable But Does Not Use msg.value, Trapping ETH
findings.description: The `payable` modifier on `permitWrap()` serves no purpose — the function uses `wTEL.transferFrom`, not `msg.value`. Any ETH accidentally sent to this function is permanently trapped in the contract with no recovery mechanism.

findings.title: Missing _disableInitializers() in StablecoinManager Constructor
findings.description: No `_disableInitializers()` call in the StablecoinManager constructor. The bare implementation contract can be initialized by anyone. While OZ v5 UUPS prevents proxy compromise, this violates best practices and leaves the implementation contract in an uninitialized state that could be exploited.

findings.title: _checkRole Bypass Overly Broad During Initialization
findings.description: The `_checkRole` override bypasses ALL role checks during initialization, not just the MAINTAINER_ROLE that is needed. Any role-gated function called during initialization would bypass its role check, expanding the attack surface beyond what is necessary.

findings.title: gitCommitHashAttested Returns Ambiguous Value That Cannot Distinguish Never-Attested from Failed
findings.description: `gitCommitHashAttested()` returns `ciPassed` instead of attestation existence status. This makes it impossible to distinguish "never attested" from "attested but CI failed" — both return false. Off-chain systems relying on this function for audit trails cannot determine if a commit was reviewed.

findings.title: MAINTAINER_ROLE Can Drain All Funds via rescueCrypto Without Timelock
findings.description: MAINTAINER_ROLE can withdraw all native and ERC20 tokens via `rescueCrypto()` with no timelock, limit, or multi-sig requirement. This represents centralization risk: a compromised MAINTAINER_ROLE key can drain the faucet entirely. Acceptable for a testnet faucet but would be a critical issue in production.

findings.title: Uniform dripAmount Applied Across Tokens with Different Decimal Precision
findings.description: A single global `dripAmount` is applied to all ERC20 tokens regardless of their decimals. This could lead to vastly different economic values being dripped (e.g., 1e18 of a 6-decimal token vs. a 18-decimal token), causing either over-generous or negligible drips depending on the token.

findings.title: receive() Accepts ETH Without Emitting Events, Hindering Monitoring
findings.description: The empty `receive()` function accepts native tokens from any sender without emitting events. This makes deposit monitoring difficult for off-chain systems and explorers, as there is no on-chain record of who funded the contract or how much was deposited.
